claims.claim: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general (economy-wide) price level; the inflation rate is the percentage change in the price level between periods, and when the price level falls the economy experiences deflation, defined as a period when the buying power of money increases.

Economists measure the price level with a basket of goods and services and express it as an index number, transforming the basket's cost into a series with an arbitrary base year set to 100; the inflation rate is then the percentage change in that index over time.

The most commonly cited U.S. inflation measure is the Consumer Price Index, calculated by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics from prices in a fixed basket of goods and services representing the purchases of a typical urban household; the CPI-U covers about 89% of the population, prices are collected in 75 urban areas from about 23,000 retail and service establishments, and its standard reference base is 1982-84 = 100 with fixed quantity weights updated every two years.

A fixed-basket index suffers substitution bias (consumers shift toward goods that become relatively cheaper, which a fixed basket ignores, tending to overstate cost-of-living increases) and quality/new-goods bias (improvements and new products enter the basket slowly).

A nominal value is measured in the dollars of its own year; a real value is adjusted for inflation using a price index. Dividing a nominal amount by the ratio of the current index to a base index (equivalently, multiplying by base-index/current-index) restates it in constant base-year dollars, isolating changes in purchasing power.

Demand-pull inflation arises when aggregate demand keeps shifting right while the economy is at or near potential output, so extra spending raises prices rather than output; cost-push inflation arises when a rise in input prices affecting many firms (for example oil or labor) shifts short-run aggregate supply left, raising the price level even as real output falls.

By the quantity equation, money supply times velocity equals nominal GDP equals the price level times real output; if velocity is roughly constant over the long run, a given percentage rise in the money supply produces the same percentage rise in nominal GDP, and when output is near potential that shows up as inflation.

Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power: it hurts holders of cash and fixed-rate lenders/savers whose nominal return does not keep up (for example a 4% deposit rate when inflation is 5% yields a real return of about -1%) and retirees on fixed incomes, while it benefits fixed-rate borrowers, who repay in cheaper dollars.

Inflation imposes costs beyond redistribution: it blurs the information that prices carry about supply and demand, and high or variable inflation creates uncertainty that complicates long-term planning and contracts; menu costs (updating posted prices) and shoe-leather costs (effort to economize on cash) are additional real costs.

Hyperinflation is an outburst of extremely high inflation; historical episodes include Russia at about 2,500% per year in the early 1990s and Brazil and Argentina above 2,000% in 1990. In Zimbabwe, the peak month of inflation is estimated at roughly 79.6 billion percent month-on-month in mid-November 2008 (Hanke and Kwok, Cato Journal, 2009), after which Zimbabwe abandoned its own currency.

Constructed worked example (illustrative CPI series with base year = 100): with the index at 100.0, 105.0, and 109.2 in years 1-3, year-over-year inflation is 5.0% then 4.0% (cumulative 9.2%). A nominal salary rising from $50,000 (year 1) to $52,000 (year 3) is a 4.0% raise; deflated to year-1 dollars the year-3 salary is $52,000 x (100/109.2) = $47,619.05, a real decline of about 4.76% because prices rose faster than pay.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Precise peak figure for Zimbabwe's 2008 hyperinflation
positions: Official statistics ceased in 2008, so the peak is an estimate
Hanke and Kwok (2009) estimate about 79.6 billion percent month-on-month in mid-November 2008 from black-market prices and exchange rates
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the figure explicitly as an estimate attributed to Hanke and Kwok (2009) and dated to mid-November 2008, not as an official statistic.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 2e, Section 22.4: The Confusion Over Inflation
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: unintended redistributions of purchasing power (cash holders and fixed-rate savers lose, e.g. 4% interest with 5% inflation gives a real return of about -1%; fixed-rate borrowers and homeowners gain; retirees on fixed incomes lose 1%-2% of buying power per year compounding); and that inflation blurs the price signals that convey supply-and-demand information, adding uncertainty. Menu costs and shoe-leather costs are standard textbook costs summarized alongside. Original prose; facts used under CC BY with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 2e, Section 28.5: Pitfalls for Monetary Policy
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports the long-run money link: the basic quantity equation (money supply x velocity = nominal GDP = price level x real GDP), velocity = nominal GDP / money supply, and the claim that with velocity roughly constant a given percentage rise in the money supply raises nominal GDP by the same percentage, showing up as inflation when output is near potential. Cited only for the one-line long-run point; the Fed's tools are owned by monetary-policy. Original prose; facts used under CC BY with attribution.
